Getting the Vivienda Mexcal look
onto the frame we have already built

F-1

The target: what makes Mexcal look like Mexcal

Six things carry this whole design — memorize them, because every decision below protects one of them:

#ElementWhat it is
1Three materials onlyMatte white render · warm horizontal wood · grey concrete-look panels. Nothing else on the facade.
2The white band + wood doorA deep white horizontal band over a full-width wood-slat garage door — the anchor of the front.
3The angled timber crownThe sloped triangular pergola on the roof — the silhouette you remember.
4Tilted fascia planesParapet and fascia edges cut at angles, not level.
5Green on the edgesPlanters built into balcony rims, plants trailing over the white.
6Light as a materialWarm LED lines recessed in grooves — under fascias outside, routed into the wood wall inside.
F-2

Where we are: the engineer's current direction

The good news: TIPSTEP's latest renders already adopt the warm cove lighting, the wood-slat gates and the layered white volumes. What's still missing from the Mexcal DNA: the angled timber crown (3), the tilted fascia planes (4), the wood garage door as a facade element (2), the grey concrete-look panels (1), and the discipline of integrated planters (5) instead of loose pots.

What a carbon copy cannot copy: Mexcal's overall massing is angled in three dimensions and ours is a rectilinear frame that is already cast. The shape stays ours. Everything else — materials, band, crown, planes, green, light — is a cladding and joinery layer that fits on the existing structure. Realistic target: 80–85 % of the look, and nobody standing on the street will count the missing percent.

F-3

The front, translated to our building

The convergence worth celebrating: Mexcal's strongest front element is a deep white band over the garage. Our structural repair produces exactly that — a 750 mm deep beam across the 9 m opening. Rendered white with a shadow groove and LED line underneath, the repair becomes the design. Nothing to hide.

F-5

Order of work, and the material discipline

  • 1 — Beam jacket (see Beam Repair). Nothing decorative touches the front before this.
  • 2 — Conduits and chases for every LED line, inside and out, marked on the elevations and photographed before plastering.
  • 3 — Arches and anchor points formed in the remaining brickwork; chandelier anchor cast/fixed.
  • 4 — Render and panels: white render + grey microcement planes + tilted fascia forms.
  • 5 — Joinery: garage door, entry door, gates — one wood, one finish, ordered together so the color matches.
  • 6 — Crown and planters once the roof story (penthouse yes/no) is decided.

The discipline that makes it read as Mexcal: three materials, one wood species, one white. Every extra color or material added "because it was available" moves the house from Mexcal toward ordinary. When in doubt, leave it white.

Wood, in Kigali terms

For the exposed pieces (garage door, entry, crown, gates): iroko or afromosia if the budget allows — stable outdoors, silvers gracefully; treated pine with UV oil as the economical option, re-oiled yearly. Whichever is chosen, use it for every wood element so the facade reads as one hand.
